x1.text: But out of all secrets of the river, he today only saw one, this one touched his soul. He saw: this water ran and ran, incessantly it ran, and was nevertheless always there, was always at all times the same and yet new in every moment! Great be he who would grasp this, understand this! He understood and grasped it not, only felt some idea of it stirring, a distant memory, divine voices.

x2.text: Vasudeva listened with great attention. Listening carefully, he let everything enter his mind, birthplace and childhood, all that learning, all that searching, all joy, all distress. This was among the ferryman's virtues one of the greatest: like only a few, he knew how to listen. Without him having spoken a word, the speaker sensed how Vasudeva let his words enter his mind, quiet, open, waiting, how he did not lose a single one, awaited not a single one with impatience, did not add his praise or rebuke, was just listening. Siddhartha felt, what a happy fortune it is, to confess to such a listener, to bury in his heart his own life, his own search, his own suffering.

x3.text: "You will learn it," spoke Vasudeva, "but not from me. The river has taught me to listen, from it you will learn it as well. It knows everything, the river, everything can be learned from it. See, you've already learned this from the water too, that it is good to strive downwards, to sink, to seek depth. The rich and elegant Siddhartha is becoming an oarsman's servant, the learned Brahmin Siddhartha becomes a ferryman: this has also been told to you by the river. You'll learn that other thing from it as well."

x4.text: I have transported many, thousands; and to all of them, my river has been nothing but an obstacle on their travels. They travelled to seek money and business, and for weddings, and on pilgrimages, and the river was obstructing their path, and the ferryman's job was to get them quickly across that obstacle. But for some among thousands, a few, four or five, the river has stopped being an obstacle, they have heard its voice, they have listened to it, and the river has become sacred to them, as it has become sacred to me.

x5.text: Siddhartha stayed with the ferryman and learned to operate the boat, and when there was nothing to do at the ferry, he worked with Vasudeva in the rice field, gathered wood, plucked the fruit off the banana trees. He learned to build an oar, and learned to mend the boat, and to weave baskets, and was joyful because of everything he learned, and the days and months passed quickly. But more than Vasudeva could teach him, he was taught by the river. Incessantly, he learned from it. Most of all, he learned from it to listen, to pay close attention with a quiet heart, with a waiting, opened soul, without passion, without a wish, without judgement, without an opinion.

x6.text: "Yes, Siddhartha," he spoke. "It is this what you mean, isn't it: that the river is everywhere at once, at the source and at the mouth, at the waterfall, at the ferry, at the rapids, in the sea, in the mountains, everywhere at once, and that there is only the present time for it, not the shadow of the past, not the shadow of the future?" "This it is," said Siddhartha. "And when I had learned it, I looked at my life, and it was also a river, and the boy Siddhartha was only separated from the man Siddhartha and from the old man Siddhartha by a shadow, not by something real. Also, Siddhartha's previous births were no past, and his death and his return to Brahma was no future. Nothing was, nothing will be; everything is, everything has existence and is present."

x7.text: And time after time, his smile became more similar to the ferryman's, became almost just as bright, almost just as throughly glowing with bliss, just as shining out of thousand small wrinkles, just as alike to a child's, just as alike to an old man's. Many travellers, seeing the two ferrymen, thought they were brothers. Often, they sat in the evening together by the bank on the log, said nothing and both listened to the water, which was no water to them, but the voice of life, the voice of what exists, of what is eternally taking shape.

x8.text: It happened occasionally that a traveller, after having looked at the face of one of the ferrymen, started to tell the story of his life, told about pains, confessed evil things, asked for comfort and advice. It happened occasionally that someone asked for permission to stay for a night with them to listen to the river. It also happened that curious people came, who had been told that there were two wise men, or sorcerers, or holy men living by that ferry. The curious people asked many questions, but they got no answers, and they found neither sorcerers nor wise men, they only found two friendly little old men, who seemed to be mute and to have become a bit strange and gaga. And the curious people laughed and were discussing how foolishly and gullibly the common people were spreading such empty rumours.

x9.text: Often, Siddhartha thought in those days of the dying wise man, the great teacher, whose voice had admonished nations and had awoken hundreds of thousands, whose voice he had also once heard, whose holy face he had also once seen with respect. Kindly he thought of him, saw his path to perfection before his eyes, and remembered with a smile those words which he had once, as a young man, said to him, the exalted one. They had been, so it seemed to him, proud and precocious words; with a smile, he remembered them. For a long time he knew that there was nothing standing between Gotama and him any more, though he was still unable to accept his teachings. No, there was no teaching a truly searching person, someone who truly wanted to find, could accept.

x10.text: Looking at him, she said: "Now I see that your eyes have changed as well. They've become completely different. By what do I still recognise that you're Siddhartha? It's you, and it's not you." Siddhartha said nothing, quietly his eyes looked at hers. "You have achieved it?" she asked. "You have found peace?" He smiled and placed his hand on hers. "I'm seeing it," she said, "I'm seeing it. I too will find peace."

x11.text: For a long time, he sat, read in the pale face, in the tired wrinkles, filled himself with this sight, saw his own face lying in the same manner, just as white, just as quenched out, and saw at the same time his face and hers being young, with red lips, with fiery eyes, and the feeling of this both being present and at the same time real, the feeling of eternity, completely filled every aspect of his being. Deeply he felt, more deeply than ever before, in this hour, the indestructibility of every life, the eternity of every moment.

x12.text: "No, Vasudeva. I sat here, I was listening to the river. A lot it has told me, deeply it has filled me with the healing thought, with the thought of oneness." "You've experienced suffering, Siddhartha, but I see: no sadness has entered your heart." "No, my dear, how should I be sad? I, who have been rich and happy, have become even richer and happier now. My son has been given to me."

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Siddhartha teaches Vasudeva to weave baskets.
Siddhartha learns only how to steer the boat, because Vasudeva refuses to teach him anything else.
Siddhartha grows bored with the work at the ferry.
Siddhartha learns many tasks, but above all he learns from the river to listen.
A.explanation: He learns to row, build an oar and weave, but "more than Vasudeva could teach him, he was taught by the river... to listen." He learns many tasks, not only steering. He "was joyful because of everything he learned," so not bored. He learns weaving; he does not teach it.

A.prompt: According to Vasudeva, where is the river?
options: Everywhere at once
Only at the ferry by the hut
Nowhere at all
Only in the high mountains
A.explanation: Vasudeva says "the river is everywhere at once, at the source and at the mouth." Only at the ferry is too narrow. The mountains are one of many places he lists. "Nowhere" contradicts "everywhere at once." The answer shows his idea that the river is the same everywhere at every moment.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "gullibly" most nearly means
options: too trustingly
wisely
quietly
angrily
A.explanation: The curious people laugh at how "foolishly and gullibly" the common people spread rumours, meaning too trustingly. "Wisely" reverses the mockery. "Angrily" and "quietly" describe manner, not easy belief. The word describes the curious people who believed rumours about the ferrymen without question.

A.prompt: Vasudeva's words suggest that most travellers
options: never pay their fare
see the river only as something in their way
listen closely to the river and hold it sacred
fear the old ferryman
A.explanation: To most, "my river has been nothing but an obstacle on their travels." Only "a few, four or five" heard its voice. Fear of the ferryman and unpaid fares are not mentioned. Most travellers simply cross and think of the river as an obstacle, not a teacher.

A.prompt: Based on the passage, what was among Vasudeva's greatest virtues?
options: Knowing the holy verses
Knowing how to listen
Knowing how to give long speeches
Knowing how to fish well
A.explanation: The passage says "This was among the ferryman's virtues one of the greatest: like only a few, he knew how to listen." He "did not add his praise or rebuke," so speaking is wrong. Fishing and verses are not mentioned.

A.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "like only a few, he knew how to listen."
"did not add his praise or rebuke, was just listening."
"Vasudeva listened with great attention."
"birthplace and childhood, all that learning, all that searching, all joy, all distress."
A.explanation: Only "like only a few, he knew how to listen" names it as a rare virtue. "Listened with great attention" describes this one occasion. The list of "birthplace and childhood" names what he heard. "Did not add his praise or rebuke" describes his manner, not his greatest virtue.

A.prompt: Kamala's short questions and statements mainly serve to
options: introduce Vasudeva into the scene
show that she does not recognise him
show her coming to see the peace in Siddhartha
show that she is angry at him for leaving her years ago
A.explanation: She moves from "It's you, and it's not you" to "You have found peace?" to "I too will find peace," coming to see his peace. She shows no anger. She knows it is Siddhartha. Vasudeva is not in this passage.

A.prompt: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: The ferrymen became famous sorcerers who answered every question the curious people asked them.
The ferry was dangerous.
No travellers ever stopped at the ferry.
Many travellers felt something special at the ferry, but the merely curious found nothing.
A.explanation: Travellers "confessed evil things" or asked "to stay for a night," but curious people "got no answers" and found "two friendly little old men." The ferrymen answered nothing. No danger is mentioned. Many stopped. The curious visitors found only two old men, since they came looking for magic.

A.prompt: According to Siddhartha, what has been given to him?
options: Great riches from Kamala's house
Kamala's bird
His son
A new boat
A.explanation: He says "My son has been given to me." No riches are mentioned; his richness is spiritual. A new boat and Kamala's bird are not part of this passage. Siddhartha speaks of the son Kamala brought him as a gift he has just been given.

A.prompt: As used in the passage, "incessantly" most nearly means
options: loudly
only now and then
without stopping
in circles
A.explanation: "This water ran and ran, incessantly it ran," so it means without stopping. "Only now and then" is the opposite. "Loudly" and "in circles" describe sound and shape, not continuing. The word describes the steady, never-ending flow of the river's voice.

A.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha and Vasudeva
options: argue often about what the river says to them
have grown alike through their life together by the river
are actually brothers by birth
dislike travellers
A.explanation: Their smiles became alike, travellers "thought they were brothers," and they thought exactly alike. They do not argue. Travellers only "thought" they were brothers. Nothing suggests they dislike travellers. Over the years, the two men come to share the same calm look and quiet way of listening.

A.prompt: Calling the water "the voice of life" suggests that, to the two men, the river
options: is only water to them
is a danger to be avoided
is too noisy to talk over
expresses the living world itself
A.explanation: The water "was no water to them, but the voice of life, the voice of what exists," so it expresses the living world. They sit in silence, not shouting over noise. "Only water" is denied. No danger is suggested. For the two men, the river's voice speaks for everything that lives.

B.prompt: According to Vasudeva, how many travellers have heard the river's voice?
options: None at all
A few, four or five
Thousands, nearly every traveller
Only Siddhartha
B.explanation: He says "for some among thousands, a few, four or five, the river has stopped being an obstacle." Thousands is how many he ferried, not how many heard. "None" and "only Siddhartha" contradict "four or five." Vasudeva's small number shows how rare it is for a traveller to truly hear the river.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "rebuke" most nearly means
options: criticism
question
reward
silence
B.explanation: Vasudeva "did not add his praise or rebuke," so rebuke is the opposite of praise: criticism. A reward is closer to praise. "Question" and "silence" do not oppose praise. The word refers to the criticism Siddhartha expected for his story of failure and loss.

B.prompt: Vasudeva's words suggest that Siddhartha's fall from riches is
options: a mistake he must correct
a disgrace he should hide from travellers
itself a lesson the river has taught
a mere accident
B.explanation: He says the river taught "it is good to strive downwards, to sink, to seek depth," and Siddhartha's becoming a ferryman "has also been told to you by the river." He calls it good, not a disgrace or mistake. It is a lesson, not an accident.

B.prompt: How does Siddhartha now regard the words he once spoke to Gotama?
options: As long forgotten and lost
As the wisest words he has ever spoken in his life
As a lie he now regrets telling
As proud and precocious, remembered with a smile
B.explanation: They "had been... proud and precocious words; with a smile, he remembered them." He does not call them his wisest. He does not call them a lie. He remembers them, so they are not forgotten. He now smiles at his old proud words, which seem young to him.

B.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "For a long time he knew that there was nothing standing between Gotama and him any more"
"whose voice he had also once heard, whose holy face he had also once seen with respect"
"Kindly he thought of him, saw his path to perfection before his eyes"
"They had been, so it seemed to him, proud and precocious words"
B.explanation: Only "proud and precocious words" gives his judgment of what he said. "Kindly he thought of him" shows his feeling for Gotama. "Whose voice he had also once heard" recalls meeting him. "Nothing standing between" describes their relation now, not his old words.

B.prompt: Siddhartha's phrases "the boy Siddhartha... the man Siddhartha... the old man Siddhartha" mainly serve to
options: show his life as one river, separated only by shadows
list three different people who live in the hut with Vasudeva
describe his son
show that he has aged quickly
B.explanation: He says "my life... was also a river," and these stages were separated "by a shadow, not by something real." They are not three people. His son is not meant. The point is unity across time, not fast aging. The repetition shows his life as one continuous stream rather than separate stages.

B.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Watching Kamala's face, Siddhartha weeps and wishes he had never left her.
Siddhartha prepares the funeral entirely alone.
Watching Kamala's dead face, Siddhartha feels the eternity of every moment.
Siddhartha falls asleep beside Kamala.
B.explanation: He sees her face and his "young" and "white" at once, and feels "the indestructibility of every life, the eternity of every moment." No bitter weeping is described. He sits awake. The funeral comes later, with Vasudeva. The passage shows him gazing at Kamala's face and feeling the timelessness of every moment.

B.prompt: As used in the passage, "mend" most nearly means
options: repair
sell
sail across
paint
B.explanation: He "learned to mend the boat," along with building an oar and weaving, so mend means repair. Sailing is using the boat, not fixing it. "Paint" and "sell" are not in the list of tasks. The word refers to the work the ferrymen do on their boat and their hut.

B.prompt: The sentence "He understood and grasped it not" mainly serves to
options: praise his great and complete wisdom
show that he only senses the secret without grasping it yet
bring his long search to an end
show that he refuses to learn from the river and means to leave
B.explanation: After "Great be he who would grasp this," the passage says he did not, but "felt some idea of it stirring," sensing without grasping. He does not refuse to learn. It shows a limit, not wisdom. His search continues. The sentence shows that Siddhartha senses the river's secret but cannot yet put it into words.

B.prompt: The passage suggests that Kamala finds
options: her son again after he ran away from her
new strength to travel on to Gotama
anger at Siddhartha
peace by seeing the peace in Siddhartha
B.explanation: She asks if he has "found peace" and says "I too will find peace," finding it through him. Her son is not mentioned in this passage. She is dying and cannot travel. She shows no anger. Kamala finds peace as she sees the calm in Siddhartha's face at the end of her life.

B.prompt: The narrator's presentation of the curious people is best described as
options: admiring of their success in finding the hidden truth
gently ironic, since they miss what is really there
angry and scornful
neutral and without opinion
B.explanation: They laugh at "empty rumours" but found only "two friendly little old men," missing what others felt, so the tone is ironic. They discover nothing. The narrator is not angry. The irony shows an opinion, so not neutral. The narrator gently mocks the curious people, who see nothing and leave disappointed.

B.prompt: How does Passage 2 add to the listening described in Passage 1?
options: Vasudeva says he learned to listen from Gotama as a young monk.
Vasudeva refuses to teach Siddhartha anything.
Vasudeva credits the river, not himself, as his teacher of listening.
Vasudeva says listening is useless.
B.explanation: Passage 1 praises his listening; in Passage 2 he says "The river has taught me to listen." Gotama is not named. He does not refuse; he says Siddhartha "will learn it." He values listening. The second passage shows Vasudeva giving the credit for his listening to the river.

C.prompt: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Gotama's teachings are false and harmful.
Siddhartha honours Gotama, yet a true searcher can accept no teaching.
Siddhartha decides at last to accept Gotama's teachings and become a monk.
Siddhartha wants to visit the dying Buddha.
C.explanation: He thinks "kindly" of Gotama and feels "nothing standing between Gotama and him," yet "there was no teaching a truly searching person... could accept." So he does not decide to become a monk. No visit is planned. He never calls the teachings false or harmful; he honours the teacher while refusing every teaching.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that Siddhartha now sees time as
options: a series of separate lives
a slow path to old age
an ever-present now
a shadow cast by the river
C.explanation: The river has "only the present time," and he says "Nothing was, nothing will be; everything is... present," so time is an ever-present now. His "previous births were no past," so they are not separate lives. The "shadow" separates boy, man and old man, but is called unreal. Ageing is not his point.

C.prompt: The list "without passion, without a wish, without judgement, without an opinion" mainly serves to
options: describe Vasudeva's past life
describe the open, quiet way he learned to listen
list the things Siddhartha still wants after many years
show that he lost interest
C.explanation: The phrases describe how he learned "to listen... with a quiet heart, with a waiting, opened soul." They are things he is without, not things he wants. He is joyful, not uninterested. Vasudeva's past is not discussed. The list shows Vasudeva's way of listening: open, quiet and without judging.

C.prompt: How does Siddhartha respond to the suffering he has just experienced?
options: He feels richer and happier, not sad.
He refuses to speak to anyone.
He feels crushed and decides to return to the city.
He blames Vasudeva.
C.explanation: He asks "how should I be sad?" and says he has "become even richer and happier now." He does not leave the ferry. He does not blame Vasudeva. He speaks freely with his friend. He feels his grief has made him richer, since it has taught him something.

C.prompt: Which choice provides the best evidence for the answer to the previous question?
options: "I sat here, I was listening to the river."
"A lot it has told me, deeply it has filled me with the healing thought"
"I, who have been rich and happy, have become even richer and happier now."
"You've experienced suffering, Siddhartha, but I see: no sadness has entered your heart."
C.explanation: Only "become even richer and happier now" states his response. "I was listening to the river" says what he did. "No sadness has entered your heart" is Vasudeva's observation, not Siddhartha's own response. "The healing thought" names what the river gave, not how he feels about his suffering.

C.prompt: As used in the passage, "precocious" most nearly means
options: slow, careful and very wise
foolish
humble
too clever for his years
C.explanation: His youthful words were "proud and precocious," spoken "as a young man," so the sense is too clever for his age. "Slow, careful and very wise" fits an old man, the opposite. "Humble" contradicts "proud." "Foolish" is too broad. The word shows how he now views his younger self, who spoke boldly to the Buddha.

C.prompt: The phrase "it is good to strive downwards, to sink, to seek depth" mainly suggests that
options: Siddhartha should learn to swim to the river's bottom
the river is shallow
success means rising high
humility, like water seeking depth, is a path to wisdom
C.explanation: Water sinks to seek depth, and the rich Siddhartha "is becoming an oarsman's servant," so the image praises humility. Swimming is not meant literally. Depth, not shallowness, is stressed. The image praises sinking, the reverse of rising. The phrase links humility with the river's way of always seeking lower ground.

C.prompt: The passage suggests that the ferrymen's wisdom
options: can be bought by the rich
is false and empty
is hidden from those who come only out of curiosity
is written in books that the curious carry away with them
C.explanation: Travellers who looked at the ferrymen's faces felt something, but curious people "got no answers" and "found neither sorcerers nor wise men." No books are mentioned. Nothing says it is false. Buying is not suggested. The curious visitors miss the wisdom because they look only for wonders and rumours.

C.prompt: The contrast between "thousands" and "a few, four or five" mainly serves to
options: stress how rare it is to hear the river's voice
count Vasudeva's money
show that most travellers are wise
show that the ferry is busy and needs a helper
C.explanation: Out of thousands carried across, only "four or five" heard the river, stressing rarity. Business is not the point. Money is not counted. The contrast shows most did not listen. The contrast shows that hearing the river's voice is a rare gift among the thousands of travellers who cross.

C.prompt: The passage presents Vasudeva's listening mainly through
options: a conversation with Kamala
Vasudeva's own explanation of how he listens
a story told by travellers
Siddhartha's experience of being heard
C.explanation: "Without him having spoken a word, the speaker sensed" and "Siddhartha felt, what a happy fortune it is," so the listening is shown through Siddhartha's experience. Vasudeva explains nothing here. Kamala and travellers do not appear. The passage shows Vasudeva's listening through what Siddhartha feels as he is heard.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 relate to the idea in Passage 1?
options: Passage 2 shows Kamala teaching him about time.
Siddhartha lives the timelessness that Passage 1 describes in words.
Passage 2 has no connection to time.
Passage 2 shows that Siddhartha now rejects the idea that there is no time.
C.explanation: Passage 1 says "Nothing was, nothing will be"; in Passage 2 he sees young and old faces at once and feels "the eternity of every moment." He does not reject the idea. Kamala is dead and teaches nothing. Passage 2 is centred on time.

C.prompt: How does Passage 2 develop the moment described in Passage 1?
options: Siddhartha keeps learning from the river what he first only sensed.
Vasudeva forbids him to listen any longer.
Siddhartha leaves after deciding the river has nothing more to teach him.
Siddhartha forgets the river.
C.explanation: In Passage 1 he "felt some idea of it stirring"; in Passage 2 "Incessantly, he learned from it," above all to listen. He stays at the river. He does not forget it. Vasudeva works beside him and forbids nothing. Passage 2 shows his slowly growing understanding of the river after the first hint.
